newsitem.title: KENYA: Eastern Zaire erupting into multi-sided conflict.
newsitem.headline: Eastern Zaire erupting into multi-sided conflict.

text.p: A multi-sided conflict is erupting in eastern Zaire, feeding on the poison between the Hutu and Tutsi tribes which led to genocide in Rwanda and is now destroying Burundi.

Africa's newest war zone has an astonishing array of combatants fighting already or poised in the wings -- Zaire's ragged armed forces, ethnic Tutsi, Hutu and indigenous militias, Burundian Hutu rebels, Rwanda's former Hutu army and the current Tutsi-dominated armies of Rwanda and Burundi.

"There is a clear need for the international community to take swift action to prevent further fighting and potential regional escalation," International Alert, a London-based group that seeks to prevent conflict, warned on Saturday.
But analysts in the "Great Lakes" region of central Africa -- mainly eastern Zaire, Rwanda, and Burundi -- fear it may be too late to prevent catastrophe.

The looming war is in an area of minimal strategic importance for the outside world, lessening hopes for tough international action to save lives -- just as in 1994 when extremist Hutus in Rwanda led a genocide of hundreds of thousands of minority Tutsis while U.N. forces withdrew and the world watched the carnage on its television screens.
The long sickness in Switzerland of Zaire's Mobutu Sese Seko, omnipotent president since 1965, is fuelling the fire.
"There is a risk of total disorder in the state of Zaire and it is linked to the sickness of Mobutu," one of the Tutsi colonels running Burundi told Reuters.
"For 30 years there was only Mobutu. In his absence all scenarios become possible, including Zaire's disintegration."
War has begun between Zaire's army (the FAZ) and an ethnic Tutsi group called the Banyamulenge who are refusing orders to leave eastern Zaire, where they settled generations ago.
Diplomats and other analysts warn that other armed factions in Zaire's North and South Kivu provinces are being sucked in.
Rwanda's 1994 genocide laid the seeds for today's crisis across the border.
One million Hutus from Rwanda, their defeated army and the Interahamwe militia who led the genocide are in eastern Zaire.
So are Hutu refugees from Burundi with their spearhead, Leonard Nyangoma's Forces for the Defence of Democracy (FDD).
All these Hutu forces are in a joint venture: retaking control of their two countries from the Tutsi armies in power.

Their method is infiltration from Zaire and their platform is the huge refugee camps right on the Rwanda and Burundi borders. The world is spending $1 million a day to feed and shelter the refugees and, by extension, their warriors.
The military in Rwanda and Burundi have not been asleep during the armed Hutu build-up in eastern Zaire.
Rwanda's post-genocide government was unprepared when local Zaireans, Hutus and the FAZ cleansed North Kivu's Masisi area of ethnic Tutsis last year.

They have not made the same mistake with the next target for Zairean and foreign Hutu chauvinism, the Banyamulenge. This group of about 200,000 ethnic Tutsis moved to the high plateau in South Kivu from Rwanda as long as 200 years ago.

Diplomatic sources say there are now several thousand Banyamulenge guerrillas, including veterans of the new Rwandan army. Zaire's accusations that many were trained and armed by Rwanda in the past 18 months are taken seriously by diplomats.
About 1,000 crossed into South Kivu via Burundi on the night of September 21-22, witnesses told Reuters.

"They had guns and bags and some of the fighters were women. They stayed in our village for a few hours and left for the plateau by foot to fight," an ethnic Tutsi refugee in Burundi, who saw them before she was driven out of Zaire, told Reuters.
Later groups have attacked Hutu refugee camps, killing a few people but more importantly clearing a mass of hostile people from Burundi's border.
The Tutsis of Rwanda and Burundi have strategic reasons to help the Banyamulenge, not just ethnic ones.

A tough ally in eastern Zaire will move the Hutu-Tutsi frontline westwards and disrupt Hutu rebel supply lines and bases. A result could be the closure of the Hutu camps or their transfer far from the border -- a central goal for Tutsis.
"The Tutsi armies in Rwanda and Burundi are saying: let's get this fight into someone else's backyard and Zaire will be much less cocky about supporting them," said an aid worker.
It is a risky strategy for such tiny countries to adopt. But they may believe that Zaire is already a stricken giant and, with Mobutu absent, incapable of mounting a military riposte.
But a military alliance between the FAZ and the Hutu rebels against the Banyamulenge would shift the balance.
If that happens, Rwanda's powerful Tutsi army -- about 50,000 strong -- might help their kinsmen despite Kigali's pledge not to enter Zairean territory.
Rwanda, Burundi and eastern Zaire are all small producers of coffee and tea.

There are gold and diamonds mined in eastern Zaire but not by big companies. Production is unlikely to be affected for long by civil war. Conflicts in Angola and Liberia proved that African warlords are efficient at extracting and selling gold and diamonds to finance conflict.
